Fig. 3 compares performance under varying rollout budgets on all six benchmarks. RSIFlow generally lies on or near the empirical Pareto frontier and achieves the highest observed score on each benchmark. This advantage is consistent with its adaptive component selection and Task–Meta co-evolution: RSIFlow reuses rollout evidence to guide targeted updates to the Task-Agent’s Model, Harness, or Artifacts, rather than relying solely on additional exploration under a fixed harness. The co-evolving Meta-Agent further distills workflow outcomes into reusable skills and refines its improvement procedure, allowing accumulated experience to guide subsequent updates. Together, these mechanisms help concentrate the rollout budget on informed workflow orchestration. Overall, RSIFlow offers a stronger performance–budget trade-off than the evaluated baselines.

We presented RSIFlow , a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.

We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix B gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.

We separate five rounds of training-stage evolution from evaluation on the fixed 744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon n n , we first complete n n evolution rounds on training batches and then evaluate the resulting frozen system. When the Artifacts route is selected, the Task-Agent revises task-specific outputs using execution feedback, and the resulting outcomes provide evidence for Meta-Skill evolution. Revised training artifacts remain local to their original tasks and are not transferred to unseen tasks. During reporting, the selected Artifacts refinement procedure can be applied to each evaluation task through one additional feedback-guided revision. The fixed-Artifacts ablation follows the same five-round training protocol, with reporting-time refinement performed only after training.

Finally, R5 shifts to Artifacts refinement. The Task-Agent uses execution feedback and prior repair guidance to edit, test, and resubmit its current code within budget, keeping the Model and Harness fixed. This targets a local output defect without an additional model-training or Harness-reconstruction step. The final reported average is 51.21%, 18.98% above R1. This measures the span from the first reported intervention to the fifth. Reusable repair guidance enters Meta-Skills; the revised code remains specific to the current task. During the fifth training round, the Artifacts route refines training-task outputs and uses the resulting revision evidence to develop the artifact-specific Meta-Skill A1. During reporting, the frozen system applies this refinement guidance to newly generated evaluation-task outputs, allowing at most one additional revision based on permitted task-local feedback before final scoring. Thus, the improvement from R4 to R5 reflects the effectiveness of feedback-guided inference-time correction supported by accumulated Meta-Agent experience, rather than the direct transfer of revised training artifacts.

Capabilities and protocols have a many-to-many relationship: the tree groups shared requirements, while protocols locate module updates. Hypothesis consistency can involve Memory organizing evidence, Inference checking compatibility, and Planning ranking informative tests; the same Memory module can support several requirements. Explorer retains node modules; Creator uses the same tree structure and consolidates its next Base Harness. Evaluation-time skills are prepared separately (Section 4.1 ); they are not stored, evolved, inherited, or routed in the tree.

The Trinity couples environment generation and Harness evolution with a frozen backbone (Figure 2 ). Explorer collects trajectories; Evolver organizes requirements from specifications and verified trajectories into a capability tree (Sections 3.2 – 3.3 ). Through Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real , Creator builds simplified, verifiable worlds; original-task evaluation measures transfer (Section 3.3 ). Explorer selectively inherits and refines reusable modules, accumulating validated updates in a fixed-topology Harness tree (Sections 3.4 and 3.5 ). The Capability-Aware Harness Router selects a compatible branch using public task information and verified experience (Section 3.6 ).

Once the capability tree is built, each node is linked to training benchmarks through shared requirements. Although the four tasks in Figure 3 differ, all require evidence verification before decisions. This motivates Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real : Evolver designs simplified training levels from node requirements, descendants, and representative tasks’ public specifications, excluding target-task layouts, private proofs, and solution traces while preserving core decision processes. Creator implements these levels using a node Harness initialized from its Base Harness or inherited parent modules, omitting aesthetic optimization to focus on task mechanisms. Evolver’s host-executed verifier pool checks node binding, execution, state transitions, rendering, and completion. Node identifiers link specifications, trajectories, and module updates, while private verifiers and public feedback guide revisions. Explorer tests verified worlds with a frozen screening Harness, admitting only those within a predefined intermediate-performance band. Otherwise, Creator adjusts difficulty along predefined dimensions. Trial counts, performance thresholds, action budgets, and retry limits are fixed in advance; worlds and verifiers remain unchanged during local training. Curricula may be reused or regenerated, while original benchmarks assess capability transfer. Appendix E.2 details the curricula for each node.

For Explorer, capability-driven RSI builds a Harness tree aligned with the capability tree. At each node, Explorer executes admitted worlds with inherited and local modules. Evolver compares successful and failed trajectories using public observations, actions, and host-assigned outcomes to identify node-specific improvements. It develops reusable modules through host-registered bindings in the six-protocol library (Section 2.2 ), refining interfaces, bounded configurations, or implementations. Updates record node, predecessor-version, episode, and executable-example references. Before local updates, the host validates evidence, ownership, interfaces, lineage, and typed input–output assertions; ancestor modules remain preserved. Bindings use public context and permitted memory under a fixed runtime policy. Multiple bindings per protocol may coexist, with model calls determining execution order. Admission verifies grounding and executability; evaluation measures performance. Creator evolves only upon verifier-detected failures. At each iteration’s end, validated proposals are consolidated with existing Base Harness modules, merging complementary modules and removing near-duplicates. Section 3.5 details persistence, selective inheritance, and consolidation.

Capability–protocol associations suggest specialization patterns, while controlled interventions show larger gains from relevant module additions and performance losses after their removal. Based on their capability requirements, we map the embodied tasks to the d → a d\!\to\!a node of the capability tree and adopt the Harness configurations evolved there. We then use Real2Sim2Real to learn task-specific skills (Figure 8 ). For each task–Harness pair, we hold the Harness fixed, run five trial-and-error episodes in the reconstructed simulator, and summarize the trajectories into skills. Self-improvement spans Gödel machines [ 87 ] , LLM systems that rewrite their own agent code [ 88 , 89 , 24 ] , automated agent design [ 90 , 91 , 92 ] , prompt optimization [ 93 , 94 , 95 ] , and learning from self-feedback and reflection [ 96 , 97 , 98 ] . With weights fixed, improvement shifts to the harness, which is synthesized from environment feedback [ 33 ] , repaired from failed trajectories [ 32 , 35 ] , self-revised [ 19 ] , optimized as code [ 18 , 20 ] , adapted at test time [ 99 ] or per task [ 22 ] , improved at the meta level [ 100 , 101 ] , and shown to lift frozen MLLMs [ 21 ] ; benchmarks and surveys map this space [ 102 , 23 , 103 ] . Closest to ours are JIT-Agent’s harness generator [ 25 ] , HarnessX’s typed primitives [ 104 ] , HSI’s per-task-family harnesses [ 34 ] , ModularRSI’s modules evolved on benchmark-disjoint tasks [ 26 ] , and the flat capability map of Harness Continual Learning [ 105 ] and regime-branched harness tree of Adaptive Auto-Harness [ 106 ] , both evolved on the task stream. Trinity instead induces a capability tree from training trajectories, shares prefixes across 44 heterogeneous benchmarks with selective module inheritance, evolves Harnesses in Creator-generated worlds that exclude target-task layouts and solutions, and evaluates on held-out benchmarks and real robots. Unlike LLM routers [ 40 ] , ours routes among capability-specific Harnesses over one frozen backbone.

Open-ended co-evolution [ 107 , 108 , 109 ] , unsupervised environment design [ 110 , 29 ] , curricula [ 111 , 112 ] , and embodied co-design [ 28 ] adapt training to the learner; Voyager grows a skill library under an automatic curriculum [ 113 ] . Loops co-evolve language agents with environments [ 114 ] , optimizers [ 115 ] , or harnesses [ 116 , 117 ] ; environment generation spans embodied [ 118 , 119 ] , tool-use [ 120 ] , and terminal settings [ 121 , 122 ] , language world models [ 123 ] , and game verification [ 124 ] . SPADE is closest [ 27 ] : one LLM designs environments with verification code and learns roles by reinforcement learning. Trinity keeps the backbone frozen and couples world generation with Explorer and Creator Harness evolution along a capability hierarchy, execution outcomes refining Explorer and verifier-detected failures refining Creator.

Candidate benchmarks were collected through agent web search over five types of source: research benchmarks released with code or data, public AI competitions, human contests and testing standards, published games and puzzle communities, and professional practice. Because a multimodal agent must perceive its world through whatever interface that world exposes, the inventory spans every input modality in which agentic tasks are posed, and each benchmark retains the observation protocol of its source. Each modality probes a different part of an agent’s capability. Image input (photographs, rendered scenes, puzzle images, and robot camera views) tests perception from pixels, viewpoint selection, and the grounding of decisions in what is seen. Video input tests evidence acquisition over time: selecting frames within a budget, tracking events across them, and understanding what happened. Boards, grids, and maps rendered as text test spatial reasoning and state tracking over a symbolic visual state; with pixel-level perception removed, a failure can be attributed to reasoning rather than to seeing. Plain text tests the capabilities a multimodal agent relies on downstream of perception: rule discovery, experimental design, planning, negotiation, and strategic interaction. Keeping all four modalities in one inventory lets visual and text benchmarks share nodes in the capability tree (Appendix B ).

Explorer plays every benchmark with the frozen backbone (Appendix D ), and each instance uses the best-scoring compatible node Harness under the Oracle setting. Every node Harness starts from H 0 , which has no learned module, and combines the inherited modules at their retained versions with the node’s local modules; a benchmark at c → \to d → \to a therefore uses the modules of c, c → \to d, and c → \to d → \to a, subject to selective inheritance (Figure 12 ). At each node, Explorer plays the admitted training levels with these modules, and Evolver compares successful and failed trajectories to create or revise local modules; the host validates evidence, ownership, interfaces, and version lineage before every update, and ancestor modules are preserved. An updated parent is inherited only if it achieves strictly more host-verified task completions than the previously inherited modules under the same validation tasks, trial count, and budget; otherwise the previous modules are kept. A local module overrides an inherited module bound to the same identifier. Module calls take public inputs and return structured advice without advancing the environment, with at most two calls per step and none forced.

Creator builds the simplified training worlds of each node with a coding harness, created per node and iteration, with a workspace for the world and an evidence directory outside it. Its Base Harness at the first iteration is H 0 extended with the pre-RSI modules listed below. Within each iteration, Creator visits the nodes top-down: the children of the root start from the Base Harness, and every other node inherits its parent’s updated modules. Each node keeps its own guidance, one construction note, and one public action budget per iteration. Verifier-detected failures trigger local evolution, and at the end of the iteration the validated proposals of all nodes are consolidated with the current library in learning order (Equation 7 ): validated revisions replace their registered predecessors; among new modules, distinct capabilities are retained, partial overlaps are merged to preserve complementary functionality, and near-duplicates keep the earlier-learned module and discard the later one. The consolidated library becomes the Base Harness of the next iteration; it is shared by all nodes and exposed as a single tool that runs one module per call. The host, not the model, supplies the inputs of each call: the build digest, the submission allowance, and, for a rule module, a measurement of the build. Fields that the host does not supply remain unknown, and missing evidence never passes. Before submission, the host reruns the applicable audits and blocks any missing, stale, or conflicting result; Creator returns errors in the frozen task design or verifier contract to their owner instead of rewriting them.

Every run uses the same frozen backbone, Claude Opus 5 [ 84 ] with adaptive thinking at low effort, and the benchmark’s native driver, which validates each action, returns the observation, and assigns the outcome. The Base Harness H 0 plays with no learned module and no skills; for H (i) , each instance uses the best-scoring compatible node Harness under the Oracle setting, together with evaluation-time skills summarized from five preparation trials of that node Harness on the benchmark. Levels, action budgets, and scoring are fixed before the first run and shared by every Harness. Each benchmark reports performance on a 0–100 scale: task-completion, win, or solve rates where episodes pass or fail; the published bounded score where one exists; and, for ALE-Bench, the rank percentile among human entrants. The Codex Harness [ 85 ] and the DeepSeek Harness [ 86 ] ran the 16 unseen benchmarks other than the real-robot versions with the same backbone and settings through their native tool interfaces. Table 8 reports every score together with each benchmark’s measure, number of distinct instances, and number of episodes; * marks environments rebuilt from source rules through agent web search. Train benchmarks use their fixed instance sets (Section 4.1 ), and ARC-AGI-3 covers the 25 games of the public set. Six unseen benchmarks run on a fixed subset of their official set: Pencil Puzzle Bench uses the official Golden 30 set, PHYRE the 50 test tasks of fold 0 in the within-template B tier, and Video-MME-v2 a stratified subset of 400 of the 800 videos (1,600 questions); DiG-bench uses 13 of the 21 public games, all games of tiers 1–3 and the first game of each of tiers 4–7; ALE-Bench uses 26 of the 40 problems and SciGym 126 of the 137 small systems, those on which the backbone’s safety layer did not refuse the task inputs. NetHack is scored after a budget of 500 steps.

2607.08124v3.text: We evaluate TTHE on six execution-grounded benchmarks, where it improves fixed ReAct-style baselines and yields inspectable grounding, verification, and recovery policies. On the evaluated BIRD dataset, TTHE achieves 48.7 % 48.7\% mean execution accuracy over three runs, compared with 12.7 % 12.7\% for the fixed baseline. A separate ten-run execution-result consistency-voting control achieves 16.0 % 16.0\% . Harnesses selected by DeepSeek for each BIRD batch also improve MiMo V2.5 and GPT-5.5 over their respective fixed-harness baselines on the corresponding batches, without further harness evolution. These results provide evidence of cross-model transfer of the evolved task-solving procedures. Search diagnostics reveal non-monotonic effects of search budget and distinguish candidate-availability limitations from selection errors. Together, these findings support executable harness adaptation as a practical path to test-time self-evolution in LLM agents.

Contributions. • We introduce Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE) , a framework that recasts test-time adaptation as evolution over executable control programs. TTHE enables an LLM agent to transform its own execution experience into harness updates, without modifying model weights or accessing final correctness feedback. • We demonstrate gains on evaluated tasks across six execution-grounded benchmarks, compare TTHE with fixed-harness repeated sampling on BIRD, and show that batch-specific evolved harnesses can benefit other execution models on the corresponding tasks. • We present inspectable harness examples, provide a conditional analysis of corrective gains and unintended regressions for a class of trace-triggered edits, and use search diagnostics to distinguish candidate availability from selection errors.

We demonstrate gains on evaluated tasks across six execution-grounded benchmarks, compare TTHE with fixed-harness repeated sampling on BIRD, and show that batch-specific evolved harnesses can benefit other execution models on the corresponding tasks.

We evaluate TTHE on six execution-grounded benchmarks: BIRD ( Li et al., 2023 ) , LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , DS-1000 ( Lai et al., 2023 ) , Terminal-Bench 2.1, and claw-eval. These cover text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, terminal-based tasks, and agentic tool use. We use fixed evaluation sets, including hard task subsets selected before adaptation; their sizes and construction procedures are given in Appendix A .

BIRD shows the largest gain, from 12.7 % 12.7\% to 48.7 % 48.7\% mean execution accuracy. Gains also occur on LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, and DS-1000, and extend to terminal-based tasks and multi-service tool use: Terminal-Bench 2.1 rises from 55.1 % 55.1\% to 67.8 % 67.8\% , and claw-eval from 48.9 % 48.9\% to 69.4 % 69.4\% . Across these settings, the same frozen backbone supports task execution, program revision, and candidate selection. The complete procedure thus obtains useful test-time harness updates without modifying model weights or introducing a separate repair model.

Executing DeepSeek’s selected harness on the corresponding BIRD batch, without further evolution, improves MiMo V2.5 from 32.0 % 32.0\% to 56.0 % 56.0\% and GPT-5.5 from 36.0 % 36.0\% to 68.0 % 68.0\% (Table 5 ). Backbone variation tests whether other models can use the evolution procedure; this experiment instead tests whether they can use its resulting programs. The gains show that a batch-specific harness can benefit execution models other than the one that evolved it.

TTHE turns test-time execution experience into updates to an agent’s executable harness, without changing model weights or accessing final correctness feedback during adaptation. Across six execution-grounded benchmarks, it improves over fixed baseline harnesses on the evaluated task sets and produces inspectable grounding, verification, and recovery policies. Transfer experiments further show that batch-specific evolved harnesses can benefit other execution models on the corresponding tasks. Our conditional analysis characterizes the balance between corrective gains and unintended regressions for trace-triggered edits, while search diagnostics show that generating useful candidates does not ensure that they are selected. Together, these findings support executable harness adaptation as a practical path to test-time self-evolution, with reliable selection under incomplete evidence remaining a central challenge.

2605.30621v2.text: In current practice, harnesses are typically designed by hand. However, such manual design is brittle in deployment-time environments: task distributions shift, edge cases appear, and useful procedures are discovered only after the system interacts with real tasks. A natural response is to update the harness automatically from execution evidence: failures, feedback, trajectories, and successful procedures can be written back into the harness and reused on future tasks. We refer to this setting as harness evolution (Fig. 1 ): the model weights remain fixed, while the external agent harness is revised over time. Recent self-evolving agent methods Madaan et al. (2023) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Agrawal et al. (2026) ; Xia et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2026c) pursue this approach across diverse harness components and have shown end-task improvements over non-evolving baselines. In these works, harness updates are typically produced by an LLM from execution evidence; we refer to this update role as the evolver .

First, harness-updating is flat in base capability . When we fix the task-solving agent and vary the evolver model, models from different capability tiers produce harness updates that lead to surprisingly similar gains, and no evolver dominates across all substrates. Our case studies further show that even the Qwen3.5-9B evolver produces harness updates whose downstream gains match those of Claude Opus 4.6, despite a large gap in base capability.

Second, harness-benefit is non-monotonic across base-capability tiers . Mid-tier models (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B) benefit most from updated harness, and strong-tier models (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6) reach the performance ceiling and benefit less. The weak-tier end, however, is not explained by the same ceiling argument: with the largest headroom above their base capability, models like Qwen3-32B might be expected to benefit most, yet they benefit the least. Our in-depth analysis identifies two failure modes that explain this weak-tier gap: (i) harness activation failure : weak models often fail to invoke relevant harness artifacts (e.g., skills) during task-solving; and (ii) harness adherence failure : even when the harness is loaded, weak models fail to adhere to it due to weak instruction-following over long-horizon tasks.

Agent Harness. We use agent harness to denote the external, non-parametric context and infrastructure through which an LLM is deployed for task execution Yao et al. (2022) ; Ning et al. (2026) ; Lee et al. (2026) . Formally, at evolution step t t , the LLM agent is defined as: A t = ( f , H t ) , A_{t}=(f,H_{t}), (1) where f f is the agent’s model backbone and H t H_{t} is the harness state after step t t . Following common harness self-evolution settings Zhou et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2026c) , we keep f f fixed and only update editable components of H t H_{t} (e.g., prompts, skills, memories), and fix other components such as tool interfaces and execution policies.
